title: Taking A Step
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett describes the Dharma transmission ceremony completed with Nomon's teacher Norman Fischer, drawing on writings from Dogen about honoring the Buddha ancestors. Nomon tells of arriving at Norman's seaside home, of Norman's wife Kathy joining the ceremonies after a fellow diver died of a heart attack on her scuba trip, and of rising at 4:30 to chant the ancestors' names with prostrations. Nomon recalls copying the lineage documents in ink on silk, wanting praise for Nomon's calligraphy, then folding the page away and joining the conversation. Nomon reads Dogen's passage on the document of heritage and reads it as an invitation open to everyone, then closes with plans for the community and a request that people take their own next step.

sentences.text: I have a friend from college named Michael Travis.
Michael Travis is like a minor rock star; he's a drummer in a jam band called the String Cheese Incident.
Maybe you've never heard of them, but they have a lot of fans.
I don't see him that often because he's like a rock star; you don't actually see your rock star friends very often.
I just happened to be with him the first time they sold out a significant venue.
It was the Great American Music Hall in San Francisco.
I remember the band kind of huddling up and saying, "We sold out the Great American!"
And they were so happy.
I feel like we sold out the Dharma Hall today.
Thank you for that.
Not like for me, but every time any of us steps forward in some way into our life, we all benefit.
In religion, we do this fabulous job creating these sort of artificial stages and containers and uniforms and all this.
There's a stage for me to step into, but why I would do that is for all of us.
We all, in some way, are stepping into that together.
What a great excuse we created to come together tonight and practice and get to do mindful sitting and walking.
I was kind of shuffling, I guess.
What a great joy it is to get to be together with so many dear Dharma friends, old and new and from near and far, and practice this way, which is really just about being ourselves.
Just about being a person, just about settling into our life the way it is, working with our resistances and our troubles in some new way, maybe, kind of as a practice.
Anyway, I appreciate that you're here for those reasons.
I feel so supported personally.
What a privilege.
I've got a big stack of cards and a bunch of emails and stuff.
It's nice.
I thought I should tell you a little bit about the Dharma transmission process, in case you're interested.
Maybe you're interested since you came, which is a sort of mysterious process.
A lot of our ordination ceremonies are actually public ceremonies.
We have a precept ceremony where you sew and receive a blue little Buddha bib.
They had a wonderful one of those just the other night in Seattle.
So it's a public ceremony.
You study Buddha Dharma and you study the precepts and you work with people in private in preparation, but the actual ceremony is public.
And our novice priest ordination is also a public ceremony.
For whatever reason our ancestors concocted the next ordination, this Dharma transmission ordination, as a private ceremony.
But private and secret are a little bit different things.
Privacy is very important for us.
Sometimes we need the safety of a private container.
For instance, in Formosan we have private interviews.
In our lives we have private conversations and private relationships, and when these are healthy, they're very important and very positive for us.
There's some water in them.
Can you get some water?
Are you sure you're okay?
But private is a little different from secret.
The Dharma transmission ceremony, I suppose, has some secret elements, but it's more private.
And so I can share a little bit with you about it, but I couldn't invite you all to go.
So my colleague Rick Spencer and I arrived in the evening.
You often do this at a temple, so we did this actually kind of a home temple, at our teacher's home temple.
So Rick and I arrived one evening at Norman Fischer's home, and his wife Kathy was there as well.
At his home he has some practice places, these little kind of huts, and the place is quite incredible.
You know how they always say that don't practice Dharma in order to gain anything?
Have you heard that?
I hope you've heard that.
You're not going to get any goodies.
Maybe you'll get the goody of getting to be yourself; that's a good goody, but not to get external goodies.

But what happened with Norman Fischer and Kathy Fisher and their family was that they, from their early twenties into their middle forties, lived essentially like monks living inside the Zen community.
Because they kind of went straight there at college, they didn't have a chance to accumulate jobs and resumes and IRAs and money and stuff like that.
They never owned a house or anything like that.
So what happened is somebody gave them a house.

So sometimes you do get something, and not just any house; they were given this house which is like on top of this really tall hill, like on the seacliff of the Pacific Ocean in this like incredible California neighborhood, little teeny kind of place.
And so this sort of little complex, some of the buildings were kind of too funky, they had to tear them down, but they have a house and you can hear the ocean the whole time.
The cliff up above, you can see the seals and stuff, and then down below there's like a little hut that's like a little zendo and a kind of little study.
So this little complex became our monastery for this ceremony because the ceremony requires some different spaces to do it.
And his wife Kathy was not supposed to be there.
It was the original plan.
And if you were at our sesshin the week before at Samish Island, you might remember Norman mentioning, I think he didn't really mean to mention it, but it was a powerful thing that happened.
So he mentioned that Kathy is a big, she's a middle school science teacher and she's also a big scuba diver.
And so every summer she goes on these incredible scuba diving expeditions all over the world, to wherever the best place is to scuba; nothing stops them.
And so she and her scuba diving buddies were in like western Indonesia, far from everything.
And they finally took like five plane trips and six boat rides and stuff like this, a long boat ride.
And they got into the water and they're very organized, methodical divers, and they'll do all the safety checks and all that.
And they got into the diver and they started their first dive.
And exactly one minute into their first dive on the other side of the world, one of the, I think there were five of them, one of them suddenly looked weird.
Something was wrong; they couldn't tell what's going on.
And it turned out he died of a heart attack right there in the water.
An instant catastrophic heart attack.
They didn't find out until later it was a heart attack.
Nothing to do with diving or diving safety or anything like that; he just died.
And so they, I won't tell you all about it, but it was very difficult, very traumatic, and he has kids and grandkids and everything.
And so they ended the trip early, came home after they took care of his body.
And so she really wasn't supposed to be there, but because of death she was there.
And several of the ceremonies include very strong language about life and death.
But this is not just like some hobby to make our life a little bit nicer.
This whole process of practicing and looking at what's really arising in every moment is about the whole wheel, the whole wheel of life and death.
So there are several times in these ceremonies that you ask the teacher; it's all usually scripted, but still powerful scripts, you know.
You say something like, "Because of birth and death we need to practice.
Please, you know, help me.
Please give me the tools and the powers to practice the great way of life and death."
And so it was sad, but it was in a way really appropriate that she was there.
It was wonderful that she was there too.
I know Kathy a little bit and got to know her better.
And the other strange thing is, I don't have to go on too long about the Fisher family, but it's interesting, you know, so many ways practice can go.

Kathy had been a monk with Norman, but then when there were sort of big changes at San Francisco Zen Center in the mid-eighties, she kind of stepped out of that life and went on to become a schoolteacher.
And just a couple of years ago, and she doesn't feel like she rejected practice, she just put her focus somewhere else.
But just a few years ago, actually starting with one of our retreats at Sam's, she kind of came back to practice.

And she was ordained and everything, and so part of the ordination process is you sew and wear this robe, which didn't mean you didn't know I had one before because it was like black on black, you know.
So now it's more obvious.
And so she had one of these, and when she came to Sam's, she kind of restarted practice.
She got on and it was like mildewy and stinky, couldn't wear it, you know.
So she's kind of just gotten back into practice.
So I know what ended up happening with her coming back early is what she and her teacher decided is she would do Dharma transmission too.
So she also did Dharma transmission, just completed last night, actually.
So that was quite something.
So birth and death was a big theme of this process.
The other themes were relationship, intimate relationship, and ancestors.
And in those ceremonies where you're asking the teacher, you're also asking in light of the ancestors.
And the whole thing kind of revolves around intimate relationships with the people that are obvious, that are here, and the people who have gone before, and the people who are coming next.
But the whole thing is sort of designed to help you really feel and experience in your body that you're not an individual person.
You're not an individual person, like trying to do practices to improve yourself.
You're just sort of one manifestation of this continually arising thing that we give different religious names, like Buddha, Dharma, or something.
And so that you do lots of stuff to reference and honor and really feel the ancestors.
And one of them is that you get up early in the morning.
In this case, we got up at 4:30, which is like not too early.
You do this at a monastery, you get up a lot earlier.
We got up at 4:30 in the morning and went around doing various incense offerings and bells and chanting the names of the ancestors.
And with the name of every ancestor, we do a prostration.
And so I'm the ninety-third generation, and every day we do this.
So lots of bowing, lots of chanting, lots of remembering the ancestors.
And then the other thing that we did to sort of clarify this relationship, and these are all things you actually do, you know what I mean?
And in a way, every teaching is in a way sort of secret because it's not really activated until you actually do it.
But the other aspect of this Dharma transmission process, it kind of comes from China.
The Chinese civilization is a very advanced early civilization.
We kind of forget that now.
We think communism, dirty pollution, something.
But actually, China is such an ancient and deep civilization.
And they early on developed very complex ways of interacting and a lot of interest also in their own ancestors.
And they had a very complex and elaborate early legal system and a sort of system of scholastic merit-based governance, which wasn't all classes of Chinese civilization.
I'm sure there are plenty of peasants.

But anyway, while our ancestors, most of us, I think, have European ancestors in the dark ages while we were crawling around in the mud or something like that, they were writing refined poetry and sitting three-day exams and drinking very good tea.
And so when Buddhism came to China and the sort of Zen movement arose out of that Buddhism, they referenced all that.
So for instance, we have these stories called koans, which are sort of interesting, sort of unique to Zen, sort of dialogue of intimate encounter and relationship.
That's sort of strange too.
And the word koan turns out to mean like a legal precedent, a legal case.
So a lot of stuff in Zen actually references the ancient Chinese legal system.
Strange, isn't this stuff strange?
Like we thought awakening, actually no, ancient Chinese law is what we're doing.
And so they were big on documents, right?
Legal system, you got to have documents.

So we created Zen documents, that's the other thing we did in our week, which are like you take this great big piece of silk, this big, this wide, and you copy with a paint brush, a pen, or a calligraphy brush, sorry, and ink these lists of ancestors arranged in very particular ways and with particular phrases and particular symbols.
And it takes like all day for three days to copy these documents.
But again, it's the ancestors; you're writing their names, you're thinking of them, and kind of like our process of sewing our own robes.

You're also kind of working through once again your personality and your stuff, and you're there, and you're trying to do it right, and you're making mistakes, and you're trying to do it better, and you're watching your own everything unfold in the middle of this solemn heist of the highs and ceremonies.
One thing I appreciated about that was I just felt very aware of my own craziness, and my own silliness, and yet you just keep going.
Like at one point I did, there was this one document that has a big kind of title.
I did it really well.
I sort of picked a script, I didn't just copy it, I did it even better.
You're copying an ancestor since, in this case I was copying a senior practitioner who had done this five years earlier, and I did even better than hers.
And when I finished I wanted to go inside and show everybody.
And so I said, "Huh, look at that.
I want validation."
So I did take it inside, but they were talking about something else.
I folded it up again and just joined the conversation.
Most of this work is done silently, and you're just looking at what is this?
What is this life?
What is this transmission in the context of these ancestors?
And one of the things we did in preparation was we studied some of the writings of Dogen, who's the Japanese founder of this school.
He lived 1200 to 1253.
And Dogen was very impressed by these same things when he went to China, and he talks about it.
And in the context of doing the ceremony, you kind of get it a little more.
He was moved by what he felt.
And for instance, before we chanted these names of the ancestors and did all these prostrations early in the morning, we chanted a little writing from Dogen.
I didn't realize it was Dogen until after I got home and saw it there.
We chanted, *Actualizing Buddha ancestors means to uphold and see them in veneration.
It is not limited to Buddhas of past, present, and future.
Those going beyond Buddhas, who are going beyond themselves, is taking up those who have maintained the face and eye of Buddha ancestors, formerly bowing and encountering them.
They have manifested the power of the Buddha ancestors, dwelt in it, and actualized it in the body.*
He has a funny style, so I'm going to read that again.
You can hear what I was just talking about is right there in Dogen.
He wrote this, I think in about 1230, so a while ago.
*Actualizing Buddha ancestors means to uphold and see them in veneration.
It is not limited to Buddhas of past, present, and future, but is going beyond Buddhas, who are going beyond themselves.
It is taking up those who have maintained the face and eye of Buddha ancestors, formerly bowing and encountering them.
They have manifested the power of the Buddha ancestors, dwelt in it, and actualized it in the body.* He ends with the body.
We sometimes think of practice as so heady, don't we?
Like, I've got to figure this out.
I've got to meditate.
And then in this particular chapter of his great book of essays, he lists off all the ancestors after that.
And then he ends by describing the same kind of situation when he was in his teacher's room, just like Rick and I were in Norman's room.

He wrote, "I saw Rujing, my late master, old Buddha Tian Tang, at the time of the summer practice period in the first year of the Baojing era, 1227, and with the formal bow, completely received these Buddha ancestors.
This can only occur between a Buddha and a Buddha."
The other big thing that we did were a bunch of ceremonies.
And in these ceremonies, using all these symbols, all these powerful religious symbols, which in a way are all made up, right?
That's what humans do, right?
They make up culture.
But I also have a certain depth and power to them, partly just through our own inhabiting them.
And part of why we have kind of a slow process, I think that we all come into Zen with some idea of gaining something and learning something and attaining something and becoming something.
And so it might sound like Dharma transmission, oh, in America we only do that after many years, and it must mean the person has really attained something, right?
It's like marking that.
So you might think that somebody's really attained something.
I think it's not that exactly, though.
There are changes, and things happen, otherwise why do this?
There's maybe some settling and some realizing something, I don't know.
But it's not like you attain some better mind or something.

It's more that why you would do this ceremony only after many years is you've had enough time to settle into your life in this context so that you can inhabit these powerful symbols without being, you know, without being sort of overwhelmed by them.
So I don't think it doesn't mean that the person becomes more special or graduated or something like that.
Panabhasa Bhikkhu, who is visiting with us today, nice to have you here, was telling me that in the Burmese Forest tradition it's just purely the number of years.
After 20 years you're a Mahatera, that's it, you know.
So just hang in there, you know.
You've got to be a monk in good standing, and it's not like they did nothing.
They did good practices and some amount of other things, I'm sure.

But, you know, so, you know, this whole thing is not, I think it's easily misunderstood as attaining something, but maybe it's more just a way of sort of enacting a kind of gradual maturity or something.
Like, you know, as children, maybe we start out when we're born in some way, sort of, you know, undifferentiated state of some kind, maybe as children, not separating things, just existing.

And then quickly we learn language and we learn if it's this, it's not that, and we separate things, and we learn that I'm separate from everybody else, and we become empowered in a way, but also isolated, right?
Also alone.
You know, there's a big root of suffering there, and that's separation.

And so maybe Dharma practice or any true spiritual practice is a kind of, you know, circling back around, feeling this non-differentiation, feeling this connection between yourself and the world, yourself and whatever symbol you need, and maybe you need Buddha, maybe you need Zen ancestors, you know, if that's your trip, you know.
Good, you know, please use them well.
Please love the ancestors.
Maybe you need another different form.
And you're not like a child again.
That's not the same.
We've somehow come around to some understanding that the language and the separation is itself just a convention, you know, not really so real as we thought.

So there's a whole series of ceremonies, and, you know, it's okay, I could tell you about them in detail, but you just forget anyway, so we won't waste our time, but some are very simple, you know, very short.
They're all private, just you and the teacher in the room.

And the other interesting thing about the Zen tradition that kind of differentiates it from other Buddhist traditions is once you have this sort of strong tradition of ancestors, then the teacher, you know, then the abbot becomes a very important figure and in a way is sort of raised up above Buddha in some ways.
And so it's interesting.
These ceremonies are all done in the abbot's room, not in the Buddha hall, not in the Zen hall, but in the abbot's room privately.
And so there are some of the ceremonies in which your teacher, in a very conspicuous way, like really stands in, sits in for Buddha.
You know, there's a special ceremonial chair and special chants are done and he sits down or she, and here she is Buddha, you know.
And you really feel it in the ceremony.
And then part of the ceremony, you know, you change places.
The student sits in that seat and you're Buddha, you know.
So, you know, does it make you Buddha?
You already were Buddha.
You already are Buddha, all of us.
The two main ceremonies at the end, one is about precepts and one is about lineage again.
And it's interesting about the Bodhisattva precepts, especially the way they're done in Soto Zen, is it's always the same precepts.
You know, it's interesting.
You would think there would be like advanced precepts.
You know, the way we think about things, right?
Like I'm a beginner now, he's advanced, he probably has, you know, it's actually the exact same precepts in all of Zen, it's kind of that way.
They say it's the same at the beginning, you know, the same at the middle, the same at the end.
But in a way it's different in a way it's the same.
And so in one of the big ceremonies in the end called Denkai, kai is the same kai as like in Jukai, so precepts.
You receive the same precepts again, the same 16, the first three about paying homage to Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.
So they actually fold Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha in as precepts.
The next three about the sort of universal aspiration to do good and benefit others.
And then there are 10 more specific ones.
If you've been around you've heard them, but if not, I just want to mention kind of the outline of it.
You know, basic stuff that's universal to all moral systems, all religions.
Not killing, not stealing, being careful about speech and the body and sexuality.
You know, all the usual stuff.
But in this ceremony it's just the same precepts again, but just done with a more powerful container, such that it empowers you to then in turn be able to give these precepts in other ceremonies.
And so that's like the sort of logistical change, I guess.
Because once you've gone through the Dharma transmission, you can yourself give precepts in our other precept ceremonies, the Jukai, the lay receiving precept ceremony, and the priest ordination.
But same precepts, you know.
So it's the same.
And you know, in a way maybe the whole design is just sort of designed to just try to get it through our thick skulls one more time.
You're okay already.
You're complete already.
Your precepts are the full precepts.
There's no secret life.
There's no other you.
There's no more, no new teachings.
But actually there are a few little secret things.
I'll tell you about those.
You know, maybe that wasn't the Buddha's plan, but who knows?
And then so that's the first ceremony.
So then you receive the precepts in a new way.
And then the second, this is sort of the penultimate ceremony, is then you receive all the gear to gear you up.
But again, pulling out all the stops with big, powerful, symbolic ceremonies.
And part of how religion works, which I've really come to appreciate, is we'll have all these things that we always do it the same way.
And you'd always do it the same way for 10 years, 20 years, 30 years.
And then at a certain point you go to a ceremony, and it's a different way.
And then it's like, "Whoa!"
And so if you hadn't already been sort of acculturated to the usual way, it wouldn't have any power at all.
But since you are acculturated to the other way, it becomes very powerful.
So like ordained people always spread this little cloth before they bow.
Which originally was a sitting cloth, as you can see.
They didn't use it the original way.
And so when you spread it out, you don't just spread it out, you spread it and you fold it in a particular way.
So in all the ceremonies in Dharma transmission, you spread it out all the way.
So it's very powerful.
And then in this final ceremony, not only do you spread it out, but you spread it out and you lay it on top of your teachers, which is like touching somebody's something.
You never would touch somebody's robes.
That's what this ceremony you do.
That's what's done.
So again, just some powerful, beautiful ceremonies.
And in that ceremony, you receive the...
And this is the kind of biggest ceremony of succession, which was invented by the Zen people.
They say they went back to the Buddha.
Where the teacher, the symbols of office, the real symbols are the robe and the bowl, the robe and the bowl.
And the earliest form of practice, the original monks, which Panabosa is practicing, that's kind of like your only possession.
So it's a big deal.
You have one bowl, which is what you eat from, and you only eat what's offered into your bowl.
And you have one robe or one set of robes.
In our practice, which is elaborated from that, the robes are more symbolic.
I don't wear this every day, but it's a powerful symbol.
So you receive the robe and the bowl and the staff, which is like an obvious symbol from kings.
This is like the Dharma King's staff, which Bob made for us.
Thank you, Bob.
You're beautiful.
And some other gear that you use in other ceremonies, but again, done privately with lots of prostrations.
The other part of these last two ceremonies is they're only done at night.
They're only done at night, and sometime around midnight is best.
That just adds, you know, you're sort of, you know, in the daytime, our sort of fantasy of separation is more alive.
But in the middle of the night, maybe better if they do it at like four in the morning or three in the morning or something, but they do it in the middle of the night.
You know, this is sort of the dream time, where these symbols are more alive and are sort of subconscious, sort of beyond conceptual life.
The life of emptiness is more present.
Logistically, some of the ceremonies involve a very dark room and lighting a candle, and you actually examine some of these documents you created in a very sort of powerful way in the dark.
So it's very, very beautiful, very powerful.

Hopefully, if some of you are very traditional practitioners, you won't be offended by me telling you all these things, but I just thought you, you know, I probably won't talk about this again, but I just thought you'd like to know what the process is and my sense, a little bit of my sense of what it might mean or what it might not mean.
Here's a little bit more from Dogen about receiving these documents.

When Dogen went to China, somehow he finagled an imitation with various abbots, or at least he says he did, at these Chinese monasteries to see their secret documents, to see their private transmission documents.
He saw several of them.
It's one of the things that scholars now are a little, in some ways, a little doubtful of this story.
It didn't seem like you'd show a New Japanese monk your documents, but he certainly saw some.
He certainly saw his teachers.
But here's what he wrote about seeing those documents:
*The meaning of the document of heritage is this.
Seeing it, you understand the sun, the moon, the stars, and inherit Dharma.
You attain skin, flesh, bones, and merit and inherit Dharma.
You inherit a robe or a staff, a pine branch or a whisk, an Udumbara blossom or a brocade robe.
You receive straw sandals and an arched bamboo staff.
At the time of the Dharma heritage, the document is handwritten with the blood of the finger or the tongue.
You can put blood in the ink.
Or it is handwritten with oil or milk.
Each one of these is a document of heritage.
Those who entrust and those who receive this heritage are both the Buddha's heirs.
Indeed, whenever Buddha ancestors are actualized, Dharma heritage is actualized.
At the time of actualization, innumerable Buddha ancestors arrive without expectation and receive Dharma without seeking.
Those who inherit Dharma are all Buddha ancestors.*
Those who entrust and those who receive this heritage are both the Buddha's heirs.
Indeed, whenever Buddha ancestors are actualized, Dharma heritage is actualized.
At the time of actualization, innumerable Buddha ancestors arrive without expectation and receive Dharma without seeking.
Those who inherit Dharma are all Buddha ancestors.
The external meaning of this seems to be you go through this week-long ceremony after twenty years and you get to do this, but I think the inner meaning is all of us are doing this all the time.
Every moment, there's this possibility of showing up, right?
This possibility of really showing up without expectation, like he says, and receiving the Dharma without seeking.
And that the Buddha ancestors are not someone else, all of us who allow that opening, that receiving, our Buddha ancestors on that moment.
This was a powerful process, and I'm really grateful to my teacher and the tradition and to all of you, but I can't tell you that I understand the sun, the moon, and the stars.
I don't know whether I've inherited the skin, the flesh, the bones, and the marrow of the Dharma.
That's not really important.
There's something deeper happening in our life than what we can think about.
Maybe one way to think about all this is a sort of development of trust, trust in something bigger than myself.
Maybe that slowly builds up as we practice steadily over time.
And maybe even despite our bright ideas and our new theories and our learning and our thinking, maybe there's some deep trust that can develop.
We can put all kinds of names on this: grace, faith, touching the mind, ground.
It does seem to take a while.
I was thinking, too, about if this is like graduating or something like that.
I started practice twenty-five years ago.
I did the math, and people here have practiced longer than that.
I was thinking, if it was about attaining something or acquiring something, if I add up all those years and all those hours, I could probably have two or three PhDs by now easy.
So it's not about that.
It's some kind of settling out.
It involves some skillfulness.
It involves some deliberation.
It involves some discipline and some choices.
You're not going to sit on the cushion and really practice just because you've sort of tripped on something.
You're not going to come to the Dharma Hall tonight just because you didn't have anything else to do.
Maybe that's the case.
There's some, you know, the mind that chooses and the mind that makes decisions and the mind that evaluates is certainly involved.
We hope that that mind can feel a little better, but there's something below that happening.
Somehow, little by little, we realize that we can take our place in the lineage and in the world.
Little by little, maybe as this trust develops, we can learn how to really trust ourselves just the way we are.
What I've been really noticing lately, and the Sangha container has been so helpful for me to learn about this, so thank you for your patience with me as I study this.
When we don't trust somebody else, it's really about ourselves.
So please study that.
When there's that sense of graspy or resistance or judgment, maybe it's really just your own self that needs to be trusted more fully.
What does all this mean for us as a community and other people here beyond just the immediate Bellingham Zen community?
Thank you so much for coming.
Well, not a whole lot.
We'll just more or less continue.
The practice is the same, right?
Having somebody in different color to robes is not, you know, a huge game changer, but maybe little by little will be helpful.
We'll keep our Zazen schedule.
We'll keep having practice periods.
It might be that I'll start leading some of those practice periods in the way that Norman has in the past.
It might be that over time I'll be the preceptor at the Jukai ceremonies, if we have more Jukai ceremonies, if people want to do that.
It might be that eventually we'll have more priests ordained by me or ordained by Kate and Michael in Vancouver who are actually this very moment.
What's the date today?
The thirteenth?
Yeah.
They're at this very moment taking eight-thirty.
They're at this very moment preparing for one of these final ceremonies.
That's wonderful, huh?
So after dark one of them will, I think tonight will be receiving this precept ceremony for them.
So yeah, so they'll also be in the same status, I guess.
Maybe our Dharma connection with Vancouver will be even stronger, of them coming to teach and do ceremonies.
And, you know, that I happen to be sitting in this seat, I just see as a strange sort of coincidence of karma, who'd have thought.
So I'll just try to do my best, and I'm sure you will, too.
But not to think that there's only so much space or something like that, or there's only so much oxygen.
All of us, you know, the invitation was here for all of us to take the next step, to take the next step in practice.
Whatever that is for us, and that's a real process of discovery for all each of us.
It may be formal things in the Zen tradition, it may be studying and sewing special things and special ceremonies, or it might not be.
It might be the next step for you is a subtle kind of inward work that none of us are even going to see, except maybe one day we'll notice, oh, you seem a little happier.
That's nice, you know.
That would be good.
But even if that doesn't happen, that's okay.

Maybe the next step for you will be, you know, in some way working with daily practice in a new way, or studying in some different way, or it might be coming more to the Dharma Hall or it might be coming less to the Dharma Hall.
We don't know.

But in some profound way, each of us noticing this invitation that's arising all the time in our life to turn towards our life a little more fully, and to see these problems and these difficulties and these conditioning and these personality traits, whatever it is, that gets your goat, not as like problems to get rid of, but as gates of the Dharma.
After the talk, we're going to chant something about Dharma gates are boundless.
Dharma gates are boundless.
We vow to enter them.
I'm sorry we didn't manage to pass out the little books.
Maybe for that we can.
So that's what Dharma transmission is.
It's for all of us.
Oh, hi, Paul.
I can see you there.
The other thing that's powerfully wonderful about Sangha practice is whenever any of us takes these steps, whether it's apparent to others or not, we all benefit.
The whole community benefits and broader than just the obvious Dharma community benefits.
So that really helps us.
And if any kind of person thinks, well, I don't deserve to be happy, do it for us, shut up already.
If you're the kind of person who thinks I have to do it for all of them, then no, no, please take care of yourself.
Don't worry about us.
So each of us needs to make that discernment, and we can help each other, too, making that discernment.
We're not on our own.

The other logistical difference, so we'll talk more about these kind of things later, I guess, is the format of individual meetings with me changes a little bit, so we'll work out how to do that logistically.
It's a little bit more formal.
May the benefit of our coming together tonight help others who need our help.
May our practice bring a little bit of more ease and a little more joy to our world and all the suffering that is here.
And let's also, after we bow and chant, please stay and we'll have a little party.
Thank you so much.
I really appreciate everyone coming in.

And if I don't get a chance during the little party, which I know I won't with so many of us, but each of you individually, please, if you don't mind, if you can accept that globally, I really so much appreciate every person coming even if you just wanted in and no idea this was happening.
Thank you.
You just wanted meditation.
So can we pass out the chant books?
It's a little more polite when people are visiting to give them what they need.
So on the second page maybe, and if you don't know this, you can just, if you do know it, you can just let the bass go by.
There's a little chant to do at the end.
And maybe we'll also, let's, let's, we'll pull all the stops.
We have time, I think.
So we'll do the closing of the Dharma chant.
And we'll do our three prostrations.
And then why don't we sing together?
Let's do the Tisarana, the refuge in Pali, at least the way we pronounce it.

verbatim.text: I have a friend from college named Michael Travis. Michael Travis is like a minor rock star. He's a drummer in a jam band called the String Cheese Incident. Maybe you've never heard of, but they have a lot of fans. I don't see him that often because he's like a rock star. You don't actually see your rock star friends very often. I just happened to be with him the first time they sold out a significant venue. It was the Great American Music Hall in San Francisco. I remember the band kind of huddling up and saying, We sold out the Great American!

And they were so happy. I feel like we sold out the Dharma Hall today. Thank you for that. Not like for me, but every time any of us steps forward in some way into our life, we all benefit. In religion, we do this fabulous job creating this sort of artificial stages and containers and uniforms and all this. There's a stage for me to step into, but why I would do that is for all of us. We all, in some way, are stepping into that together. What a great excuse we created to come together tonight and practice and get to do mindful sitting and walking.

I was kind of like shuffling, I guess. What a great joy it is to get to be together with so many dear Dharma friends, old and new and from near and far, and practice this way, which is really just about being ourself. Just about being a person. Just about settling into our life the way it is. Working with our resistances and our troubles in some new way, maybe. Kind of as a practice. Anyway, I appreciate that you're here for those reasons.

I feel so supported personally. What a privilege. I've got a big stack of cards and a bunch of emails and stuff. It's nice. I thought I should tell you a little bit about the Dharma transmission process, in case you're interested. Maybe you're interested since you came. Which is a sort of mysterious process. A lot of our ordination ceremonies are actually public ceremonies. We have a precept ceremony where you sew and receive a blue little Buddha bib.

They had a wonderful one of those just the other night in Seattle. So it's a public ceremony. You study Buddha Dharma and you study the precepts and you work with people in private, in preparation, but the actual ceremony is public. And our novice priest ordination is also a public ceremony. And for whatever reason our ancestors concocted the next ordination, this Dharma transmission ordination, as a private ceremony. But private and secret are a little bit different things.

Privacy is very important for us. Sometimes we need the safety of a private container. For instance, in Formosan we have private interviews. In our lives we have private conversations and private relationships. And when these are healthy, they're very important and very positive for us. There's some water in them. Can you get Dove some water? Are you sure you're okay?

But private is a little different from secret. The Dharma transmission ceremony, I suppose, has some secret elements, but it's more private. And so I can share a little bit with you about it, but I couldn't invite you all to go. So my colleague Rick Spencer and I arrived in the evening. You often do this at a temple, so we did this actually kind of a home temple, at our teacher's home temple. So Rick and I arrived one evening at Norman Fischer's home, and his wife Kathy was there as well. And at his home he has some practice places, these little kind of huts. And the place is quite incredible.

You know how they always say that don't practice Dharma in order to gain anything? Have you heard that? I hope you've heard that. You're not going to get any goodies. Maybe you'll get the goody of getting to be yourself. That's a good goody. But not to get external goodies. But what happened with Norman Fischer and Kathy Fisher and their family was that they, from their early 20s into their middle 40s, lived essentially like monks living inside the Zen community.

And because they kind of went straight there at a college, they didn't have a chance to accumulate jobs and resumes and IRAs and money and stuff like that. They never owned a house or anything like that. So what happened is somebody gave them a house. So sometimes you do get something. And not just any house, they were given this house which is like on top of this really tall hill, like on the seacliff of the Pacific Ocean in this like incredible California neighborhood, little teeny kind of place.

And so this sort of little complex, some of the buildings were kind of too funky, they had to tear them down, but they have a house and you can hear the ocean the whole time. The cliff up above, you can see the seals and stuff. And then down below there, there's like a little hut that's like a little zendo and a kind of little study. So this little complex became our monastery for this ceremony because the ceremony requires some different spaces to do it. And his wife Kathy was not supposed to be there. It was the original plan.

And if you were at our sesshin the week before at Samish Island, you might remember Norman mentioning, I think he didn't really mean to mention it, but it was a powerful thing that happened. So he mentioned that Kathy is a big, she's a middle school science teacher and she's also a big scuba diver. And so every summer she goes on these incredible scuba diving expeditions all over the world, to wherever the best place is to scuba, nothing stops them. And so she and her scuba diving buddies were in like western Indonesia, far from everything.

And they finally took like five plane trips and six boat rides and stuff like this, a long boat ride. And they got into the water and they're very organized, methodical divers and they'll do all the safety checks and all that. And they got into the diver and they started their first dive. And exactly one minute into their first dive on the other side of the world, one of the, I think there were five of them, one of them suddenly looked weird. Something was wrong. They couldn't tell what's going on. And it turned out he died of a heart attack right there in the water.

An instant catastrophic, you know, heart attack. They didn't find out until later it was a heart attack. Nothing to do with diving or diving safety or anything like that, he just died. And so they, I won't tell you all about it, but it was very difficult, very traumatic and he has kids and grandkids and everything. And so they ended the trip early, came home after they took care of his body. And so she really wasn't supposed to be there, but because of death she was there. And several of the ceremonies include very strong language about life and death.

But this is not just like some hobby to make our life a little bit nicer. This whole process of practicing and looking at what's really arising on every moment is about the whole wheel, the whole wheel of life and death. So there are several times in these ceremonies that you ask the teacher, it's all usually scripted but still powerful scripts, you know. You say something like, you know, because of birth and death we need to practice. Please, you know, help me. Please give me the tools and the powers to practice the great way of life and death.

And so it was sad, but it was in a way really appropriate that she was there. It was wonderful that she was there too. I know Kathy a little bit and got to know her better. And the other strange thing is, I don't have to go on too long about the Fisher family, but it's interesting, you know. So many ways practice can go. Kathy had been a monk with Norman, but then when there were sort of big changes at San Francisco Zen Center in the mid-80s,

she kind of stepped out of that life and went on to become a schoolteacher. And just a couple of years ago, and she doesn't feel like she rejected practice, she just put her focus somewhere else. But just a few years ago, actually starting with one of our retreats at Sam's, she kind of came back to practice. And she was ordained and everything, and so part of the ordination process is you sew and wear this robe, which didn't mean you didn't know I had one before

because it was like black on black, you know. So now it's more obvious. And so she had one of these, and when she came to Sam's, she kind of restarted practice. She got on and it was like mildewy and stinky. Couldn't wear it, you know. So she's kind of just gotten back into practice. So I know what ended up happening with her coming back early

is what she and her teacher decided is she would do Dharma transmission too. So she also did Dharma transmission, just completed last night, actually. So that was quite something. So birth and death was a big theme of this process. The other themes were relationship, intimate relationship, and ancestors. And in those ceremonies where you're asking the teacher, you're also asking in light of the ancestors. And the whole thing kind of revolves around intimate relationships

with the people that are obvious, that are here, and the people who have gone before, and the people who are coming next. But the whole thing is sort of designed to help you really feel and experience in your body that you're not an individual person. You're not an individual person, like trying to do practices to improve yourself. You're just sort of one manifestation of this continually arising thing that we give different religious names, like Buddha, Dharma, or something.

And so that you do lots of stuff to reference and honor and really feel the ancestors. And one of them is that you get up early in the morning. In this case, we got up at 4.30, which is like not too early. You do this at a monastery, you get up a lot earlier. We got up at 4.30 in the morning and went around doing various incense offerings and bells and chanting the names of the ancestors.

And with the name of every ancestor, we do a prostration. And so I'm the 93rd generation, and every day we do this. So lots of bowing, lots of chanting, lots of remembering the ancestors. And then the other thing that we did to sort of clarify this relationship, and these are all things you actually do, you know what I mean? And in a way, every teaching is in a way sort of secret because it's not really activated until you actually do it. But the other aspect of this Dharma transmission process,

it kind of comes from China. The Chinese civilization is a very advanced early civilization. We kind of forget that now. We think communism, dirty pollution, something. But actually, China is such an ancient and deep civilization. And they early on developed very complex ways of interacting and a lot of interest also in their own ancestors. And they had a very complex and elaborate early legal system and a sort of system of scholastic merit-based governance,

which wasn't all classes of Chinese civilization. I'm sure there are plenty of peasants. But anyway, while our ancestors, most of us, I think, have European ancestors, in the dark ages while we were crawling around in the mud or something like that, they were writing refined poetry and sitting three-day exams and drinking very good tea. And so when Buddhism came to China and the sort of Zen movement arose out of that Buddhism, they referenced all that. So for instance, we have these stories called koans,

which are sort of interesting, sort of unique to Zen, sort of dialogue of intimate encounter and relationship. That's sort of strange too. And the word koan turns out to mean like a legal precedent, a legal case. So a lot of stuff in Zen actually references the ancient Chinese legal system. Strange, isn't this stuff strange? Like we thought awakening, actually no, ancient Chinese law is what we're doing. And so they were big on documents, right?

Legal system, you got to have documents. So we created Zen documents, that's the other thing we did in our week, which are like you take this great big piece of silk, this big, this wide, and you copy with a paint brush, a pen, or a calligraphy brush, sorry, and ink these lists of ancestors arranged in very particular ways and with particular phrases and particular symbols. And it takes like all day for three days to copy these documents. But again, it's the ancestors, you're writing their names, you're thinking of them. And kind of like our process of sewing our own robes,

you're also kind of working through once again your personality and your stuff, and you're there, and you're trying to do it right, and you're making mistakes, and you're trying to do it better, and you're watching your own everything unfold in the middle of this solemn heist of the highs and ceremonies. One thing I appreciated about that was I just felt very aware of my own craziness, and my own silliness, and yet you just keep going. Like at one point I did like there was this one document that has a big kind of title. I did it really well. I sort of picked a script, I didn't just copy it, I did it even better.

You're copying an ancestor since, in this case I was copying a senior practitioner who had done this five years earlier, and I did even better than hers. And when I finished I wanted to go inside and show everybody. And so I said, huh, look at that. I want validation. So I did take it inside, but they were talking about something else. I folded it up again and just joined the conversation. You know, most of this work done silently, and you're just looking at what is this? What is this life? What is this transmission in the context of these ancestors?

And one of the things we did in preparation was we studied some of the writings of Dogen, who's the Japanese founder of this school. He lived 1200 to 1253. And Dogen was very impressed by these same things when he went to China and he talks about it. And in the context of doing the ceremony you kind of get it a little more. He was moved by what he felt. And for instance, before we chanted these names of the ancestors and did all these prostrations early in the morning,

we chanted a little writing from Dogen. I didn't realize it was Dogen until after I got home and saw it there. We chanted, Actualizing Buddha ancestors means to uphold and see them in veneration. It is not limited to Buddhas of past, present, and future. Those going beyond Buddhas, who are going beyond themselves, is taking up those who have maintained the face and eye of Buddha ancestors, formerly bowing and encountering them.

They have manifested the power of the Buddha ancestors, dwelt in it, and actualized it in the body. So he has a funny style, so I'm going to read that again. You can hear what I was just talking about is right there in Dogen. He wrote this I think in about 1230, so a while ago. Actualizing Buddha ancestors means to uphold and see them in veneration. It is not limited to Buddhas of past, present, and future, but is going beyond Buddhas, who are going beyond themselves.

It is taking up those who have maintained the face and eye of Buddha ancestors, formerly bowing and encountering them. They have manifested the power of the Buddha ancestors, dwelt in it, and actualized it in the body. He ends with the body. We sometimes think of practice as so heady, don't we? Like, I've got to figure this out. I've got to meditate. And then in this particular chapter of his great book of essays,

he lists off all the ancestors after that. And then he ends by describing the same kind of situation when he was in his teacher's room, just like Rick and I were in Norman's room. He wrote, I saw Rujing, my late master, old Buddha Tian Tang, at the time of the summer practice period in the first year of the Baojing era, 1227, and with the formal bow, completely received these Buddha ancestors. This can only occur between a Buddha and a Buddha. And the other big thing that we did were a bunch of ceremonies.

And in these ceremonies, using all these symbols, all these powerful religious symbols, which in a way are all made up, right? That's what humans do, right? They make up culture. But I also have a certain depth and power to them, partly just through our own inhabiting them. And part of why we have kind of a slow process, I think that we all come into Zen with some idea of gaining something and learning something

and attaining something and becoming something. And so it might sound like Dharma transmission, oh, in America we only do that after many years, and it must mean the person has really attained something, right? It's like marking that. So you might think that somebody's really attained something. I think it's not that exactly, though. You know, there are changes, and things happen, otherwise why do this?

There's maybe some settling and some realizing something, I don't know. But it's not like you attain some better mind or something. It's more that why you would do this ceremony only after many years is you've had enough time to settle into your life in this context so that you can inhabit these powerful symbols without being, you know, without being sort of overwhelmed by them. So I don't think it doesn't mean that the person becomes more special or graduated or something like that.

Panabhasa Bhikkhu who is visiting with us today, nice to have you here, was telling me that in the Burmese Forest tradition it's just purely the number of years. After 20 years you're a Mahatera, that's it, you know. So just hang in there, you know. You know, you've got to be a monk in good standing, and it's not like they did nothing. They did good practices and some amount of other things, I'm sure.

But, you know, so, you know, this whole thing is not, I think it's easily misunderstood as attaining something, but maybe it's more just a way of sort of enacting a kind of gradual maturity or something. Like, you know, as children, maybe we start out when we're born in some way, sort of, you know, undifferentiated state of some kind, maybe as children, not separating things, just existing.

And then quickly we learn language and we learn if it's this, it's not that, and we separate things, and we learn that I'm separate from everybody else, and we become empowered in a way, but also isolated, right? Also alone. You know, there's a big root of suffering there, and that's separation. And so maybe Dharma practice or any true spiritual practice

is a kind of, you know, circling back around, feeling this non-differentiation, feeling this connection between yourself and the world, yourself and whatever symbol you need, and maybe you need Buddha, maybe you need Zen ancestors, you know, if that's your trip, you know. Good, you know, please use them well. Please love the ancestors.

Maybe you need another different form. And you're not like a child again. That's not the same. We've somehow come around to some understanding that the language and the separation is itself just a convention, you know, not really so real as we thought. So there's a whole series of ceremonies, and, you know, it's okay,

I could tell you about them in detail, but you just forget anyway, so we won't waste our time, but some are very simple, you know, very short. They're all private, just you and the teacher in the room. And the other interesting thing about the Zen tradition that kind of differentiates it from other Buddhist traditions is once you have this sort of strong tradition of ancestors, then the teacher, you know,

then the abbot becomes a very important figure and in a way is sort of raised up above Buddha in some ways. And so it's interesting. These ceremonies are all done in the abbot's room, not in the Buddha hall, not in the Zen hall, but in the abbot's room privately. And so there are some of the ceremonies in which your teacher, in a very conspicuous way,

like really stands in, sits in for Buddha. You know, there's a special ceremonial chair and special chants are done and he sits down or she, and here she is Buddha, you know. And you really feel it in the ceremony. And then part of the ceremony, you know, you change places. The student sits in that seat and you're Buddha, you know.

So, you know, does it make you Buddha? You already were Buddha. You already are Buddha, all of us. The two main ceremonies at the end, one is about precepts and one is about lineage again. And it's interesting about the Bodhisattva precepts, especially the way they're done in Soto Zen, is it's always the same precepts.

You know, it's interesting. You would think there would be like advanced precepts. You know, the way we think about things, right? Like I'm a beginner now, he's advanced, he probably has, you know, it's actually the exact same precepts in all of Zen, it's kind of that way. They say it's the same at the beginning,

you know, the same at the middle, the same at the end. But in a way it's different in a way it's the same. And so in one of the big ceremonies in the end called Denkai, kai is the same kai as like in Jukai, so precepts. You receive the same precepts again,

the same 16, the first three about paying homage to Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. So they actually fold Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha in as precepts. The next three about the sort of universal aspiration to do good and benefit others.

And then there are 10 more specific ones. And so if you've been around you've heard them, but if not, I just want to mention kind of the outline of it. You know, basic stuff that's universal to all moral systems, all religions. Not killing, not stealing, being careful about speech

and the body and sexuality. You know, all the usual stuff. But in this ceremony it's just the same precepts again, but just done with a more powerful container, such that it empowers you to then in turn be able to give these precepts in other ceremonies.

And so that's like the sort of logistical change, I guess. Because once you've gone through the Dharma transmission, you can yourself give precepts in our other precept ceremonies. The Jukai, the lay receiving precept ceremony, and the priest ordination.

But same precepts, you know. So it's the same. And you know, in a way maybe the whole design is just sort of designed to just try to get it through our thick skulls one more time. You're okay already. You're complete already.

Your precepts are the full precepts. There's no secret life. There's no other you. There's no more, no new teachings. But actually there are a few little secret things. I'll tell you about those. You know, maybe that wasn't

the Buddha's plan, but who knows? And then so that's the first ceremony. So then you receive the precepts in a new way. And then the second, this is sort of the penultimate ceremony, is then you receive all the gear to gear you up.

But again, pulling out all the stops with big, powerful, symbolic ceremonies. And part of how religion works, which I've really come to appreciate, is we'll have all these things that we always do it the same way. And you'd always do it the same way for 10 years, 20 years, 30 years.

And then at a certain point you go to a ceremony, and it's a different way. And then it's like, whoa! And so if you hadn't already been sort of acculturated to the usual way, it wouldn't have any power at all. But since you are acculturated

to the other way, it becomes very powerful. So like ordained people always spread this little cloth before they bow. Which originally was a sitting cloth, as you can see. They didn't use it the original way.

And so when you spread it out, you don't just spread it out, you spread it and you fold it in a particular way. So in all the ceremonies in Dharma transmission, you spread it out all the way. So it's very powerful.
And then in this final ceremony, not only do you spread it out, but you spread it out and you lay it on top of your teachers. Which is like touching somebody's something. You never would touch
somebody's robes. That's what this ceremony you do. That's what's done. So again, just some powerful, beautiful ceremonies. And in that ceremony, you receive the... And this is the kind of
biggest ceremony of succession, which was invented by the Zen people. They say they went back to the Buddha. Where the teacher, the symbols of office, the real symbols are
the robe and the bowl, the robe and the bowl. And the earliest form of practice, the original monks, which Panabosa is practicing, that's kind of like your only possession. So it's a big deal.
You have one bowl, which is what you eat from, and you only eat what's offered into your bowl. And you have one robe or one set of robes. And so in our practice, which is elaborated from that,

the robes are more symbolic. I don't wear this every day, but it's a powerful symbol. So you receive the robe and the bowl and the staff, which is like an obvious symbol from kings, right? So this is like the Dharma King's staff,
which Bob made for us. Thank you, Bob. You're beautiful. And some other gear that you use in other ceremonies. But again, done privately with lots of prostrations. Oh, and the other part
of these last two ceremonies is they're only done at night. They're only done at night. And sometime around midnight is best. So that just adds, you know, you're sort of, you know, in the daytime,

our sort of fantasy of separation is more alive, right? But in the middle of the night, maybe better if they do it at like four in the morning or three in the morning or something, but they do it in the middle of the night.
You know, this is sort of the dream time, right? Where these symbols are more alive and are sort of subconscious, you know, sort of beyond conceptual life. The life of emptiness is more present.

And just logistically, some of the ceremonies involve a very dark room and lighting a candle, and you actually examine some of these documents you created in a very sort of powerful way in the dark, you know.
So it's very, very beautiful, very powerful. So hopefully, if some of you are very traditional practitioners, you won't be offended by me telling you all these things, but I just thought you,
you know, I probably won't talk about this again, but I just thought you'd like to know what the process is and my sense, a little bit of my sense of what it might mean

or what it might not mean. Here's a little bit more from Dogen about receiving these documents. When Dogen went to China, somehow he finagled an imitation with various abbots, or at least he says he did,

at these Chinese monasteries to see their secret documents, to see their private transmission documents. And he saw several of them. And it's one of the things that scholars now are a little, in some ways,
a little doubtful of this story. It didn't seem like you'd show a New Japanese monk your documents, but I mean, he certainly saw some. He certainly saw his teachers. But here's what he wrote

about seeing those documents. The meaning of the document of heritage is this. Seeing it, you understand the sun, the moon, the stars, and inherit Dharma. You attain skin, flesh, bones, and merit and inherit Dharma.
You inherit a robe or a staff, a pine branch or a whisk, an Udumbara blossom or a brocade robe. You receive straw sandals and an arched bamboo staff. At the time of the Dharma heritage,
the document is handwritten with the blood of the finger or the tongue. You can put blood in the ink. Or it is handwritten with oil or milk. Each one of these is a document of heritage.
Those who entrust and those who receive this heritage are both the Buddha's heirs. Indeed, whenever Buddha ancestors are actualized, Dharma heritage is actualized. At the time of actualization,
innumerable Buddha ancestors arrive without expectation and receive Dharma without seeking. Those who inherit Dharma are all Buddha ancestors. Let's do that last paragraph again.
Those who entrust and those who receive this heritage are both the Buddha's heirs. Indeed, whenever Buddha ancestors are actualized, Dharma heritage is actualized. At the time of actualization,
innumerable Buddha ancestors arrive without expectation. And receive Dharma without seeking. Those who inherit Dharma are all Buddha ancestors. And so the external meaning of this seems to be
you go through this week-long ceremony after 20 years and you get to do this, but I think the inner meaning is all of us are doing this all the time. Every moment,
there's this possibility of showing up, right? This possibility of really showing up without expectation, like he says, and receiving the Dharma without seeking. And that the Buddha ancestors

are not someone else, all of us who allow that opening, that receiving, our Buddha ancestors on that moment. Because this was a powerful process and I'm really grateful to my teacher and the tradition
and to all of you, but I can't tell you that I understand the sun, the moon, and the stars. I don't know whether I've inherited the skin, the flesh, the bones, and the marrow of the Dharma.
That's not really important. There's something deeper happening in our life than what we can think about. And maybe one way to think about all this is a sort of development of trust.
Trust in something bigger than myself. Maybe that slowly builds up as we practice steadily over time. And maybe even despite our bright ideas and our new theories
and our learning and our thinking, maybe there's some deep trust that can develop. And we can put all kinds of names on this. Grace, faith, touching the mind, ground.
And it does seem to take a while. I was thinking, too, about if this is like graduating or something like that. I started practice 25 years ago. I did the math.
And people here have practiced longer than that. I was thinking, if it was about attaining something or acquiring something, if I add up all those years and all those hours,
